value.overview: Markham’s Storm-Petrel (Hydrobates markhami) is a dark, ocean-going seabird of the eastern Pacific. It spends most of its life at sea and comes ashore mainly to breed in desert regions of coastal Peru and northern Chile. The species is poorly known because it is difficult to observe away from colonies and is usually active around breeding sites at night. In Costa Rica, it is a scarce pelagic migrant recorded over Pacific waters, including around Isla del Coco.
value.classification: It belongs to the storm-petrel family Hydrobatidae and the order Procellariiformes. The accepted scientific name is Hydrobates markhami; older literature may use Oceanodroma markhami.
value.identification: This is a medium-sized, slender storm-petrel with almost entirely dark brown to blackish plumage. A pale gray or whitish diagonal bar across the upper wing is often visible in good views. The rump may appear slightly paler, and the tail is slightly forked. It flies with rapid wingbeats interspersed with glides, often close to the sea surface. Identification at sea can be difficult, especially where it overlaps with Black and other dark storm-petrels.
value.rangeHabitat: Markham’s Storm-Petrel breeds in arid coastal areas of Peru and northern Chile, where it nests in natural cavities, rock crevices, and sheltered spaces in desert terrain. Outside the breeding season it occupies open tropical and subtropical Pacific waters, often far from land. In Costa Rica it is not a resident coastal or terrestrial bird; it occurs as a marine migrant over the Pacific, with documented records from offshore waters and the Isla del Coco region. It is most likely to be encountered during pelagic surveys or boat trips.
value.migrationStatus: Migratory. After breeding in the deserts of Peru and Chile, individuals disperse through the eastern Pacific. Costa Rica is a nonbreeding passage and marine-use area, with records from Pacific waters and around Isla del Coco rather than from the mainland interior.
value.breeding: Breeding colonies are located in extremely dry coastal desert landscapes, especially in northern Chile and Peru. The species nests in cracks, crevices, and other protected cavities, generally returning to colonies at night. It lays a single egg, as is typical of many procellariiform seabirds, and both adults contribute to incubation and chick care. Breeding colonies can be difficult to detect because birds spend daylight hours at sea and visit nesting sites mainly after dark.
value.dietFeeding: Its diet is believed to consist mainly of small marine organisms, including planktonic crustaceans, small fish, and cephalopods, with other soft-bodied prey taken opportunistically. It forages from the sea surface and may pick prey from the water while fluttering or gliding. Like other storm-petrels, it can concentrate around productive ocean fronts, upwelling areas, floating organic matter, and feeding seabird groups.
value.behavior: Markham’s Storm-Petrel is highly pelagic and normally avoids land outside the breeding season. Its flight is light and fluttering, with frequent glides and banking close to the water. It is generally solitary or occurs in small groups, although larger concentrations may form where food is abundant. Adults return to colonies after dark, which reduces exposure to many daytime predators. The species is often under-recorded because of its remote habitat and resemblance to other dark storm-petrels.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered to be declining. Available estimates and monitoring remain limited, so the exact rate and geographic pattern of decline are uncertain.
conservation.threats: Important threats include introduced predators and disturbance at breeding colonies, artificial lighting that can disorient fledglings, habitat degradation in coastal desert nesting areas, and mortality associated with fishing operations. Marine pollution, plastic ingestion, oil contamination, and changes in ocean productivity may add further pressure. Because Costa Rica supports migrants at sea, local risks may include accidental capture, pollution, and disturbance from intensive offshore activities.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect and monitor breeding colonies in Peru and Chile, prevent the introduction of rats and other predators, and reduce artificial lighting near nesting areas. Improve monitoring of pelagic seabirds in Costa Rican Pacific waters, including around Isla del Coco, and promote fishing practices that reduce seabird bycatch. Reducing plastic and oil pollution, safeguarding marine protected areas, and reporting well-documented sightings can also support conservation and improve knowledge of this poorly studied species.
